content: Primary fallopian tube cancer (PFTC), commonly referred to as tubal cancer, is a malignant tumor that originates in the fallopian tubes. Between 1998 and 2003, the incidence rate was reported as 41 cases per 100,000 women. The demographic distribution of PFTC is similar to that of ovarian cancer, with the highest incidence observed in white, non-Hispanic women aged 60 to 79 years. However, recent evidence suggests that tubal cancer may be more common than previously thought. Individuals with BRCA1 and BRCA2 gene mutations are at significantly higher risk of developing PFTC. The most prevalent histological type of fallopian tube cancer is adenocarcinoma. In a large study of 3,051 cases reported by Stewart et al., 88% of cases were classified as adenocarcinomas. Among these, half were poorly differentiated, 89% were unilateral, and the distribution of disease extension was approximately one-third each for local, regional, and distant spread. Less common forms of tubal neoplasms include leiomyosarcoma and transitional cell carcinoma. Due to the anatomical proximity of the fallopian tubes to the ovaries, it is often the pathologist, rather than the surgeon, who determines the tubal origin of the lesion. Secondary tubal cancer typically arises from primary malignancies of the ovaries, endometrium, gastrointestinal tract, peritoneum, or breast. The internal location of the fallopian tubes makes early diagnosis challenging. Symptoms are often nonspecific and may include pelvic pain, vaginal discharge, or abnormal vaginal bleeding. A pelvic mass may be identified during a routine gynecological examination. Vaginal discharge associated with fallopian tube carcinoma can result from intermittent hydrosalpinx, a condition referred to as hydrops tubae profluens. Diagnosis of fallopian tube cancer may involve a pelvic examination to detect an adnexal mass. A CA-125 blood test, while nonspecific, is often elevated in patients with tubal cancer. More definitive diagnostic tools include gynecologic ultrasound, CT scans, or MRI of the pelvis. Occasionally, early-stage fallopian tube cancer is discovered incidentally during pelvic surgery. The primary treatment for fallopian tube cancer is surgical intervention, which is similar to the approach used for ovarian cancer. Since the tumor often spreads first to the adjacent uterus and ovaries, a total abdominal hysterectomy is typically performed. This procedure involves the removal of the uterus, cervix, ovaries, and fallopian tubes. Additionally, peritoneal washings are collected, the omentum is excised, and pelvic and para-aortic lymph nodes are sampled. Surgical staging and pathological findings guide subsequent treatment decisions. In advanced cases where the cancer has metastasized to other organs and cannot be completely resected, cytoreductive surgery is performed to reduce tumor burden and facilitate further treatments. Surgery is usually followed by adjuvant chemotherapy, often platinum-based. Radiation therapy has also been used with some success for palliative or curative purposes in patients with tubal cancer. Staging of fallopian tube cancer is performed during surgery using the FIGO (International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics) staging system. Prognosis largely depends on the stage of the disease at diagnosis. In 1991, it was reported that approximately 50% of patients with advanced-stage disease survived for five years when treated with surgery followed by cisplatin-based chemotherapy.
